6 tn Or &quot;in that day&quot; (KJV). 7 tn Heb &quot;and the vegetation of the Lord will become beauty and honor.&quot; Many English versions understand the phrase צֶמַח יְהוָה (tsemakh yÿhvah) as a messianic reference and render it, &quot;the Branch of the Lord&quot; (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT, and others). Though צֶמַח (tsemakh) is used by later prophets of a royal descendant (Jer 23;5; 33:15; Zech 3:8; 6:12), those passages contain clear contextual indicators that a human ruler is in view and that the word is being used in a metaphorical way of offspring. However, in Isa 4:2 there are no such contextual indicators. To the contrary, in the parallel structure of the verse צֶמַח יְהוָה corresponds to &quot;produce of the land,&quot; a phrase that refers elsewhere exclusively to literal agricultural produce (see Num 13:20, 26; Deut 1:25). In the majority of its uses צֶמַח refers to literal crops or vegetation (in Ps 65:10 the Lord is the source of this vegetation). A reference to the Lord restoring crops would make excellent sense in Isa 4 and the prophets frequently included this theme in their visions of the future age (see Isa 30:23-24; 32:20; Jer 31:12; Ezek 34:26-29; and Amos 9:13-14). 8 tn Heb &quot;and the fruit of the land will become pride and beauty for the remnant of Israel.&quot;

1 sn That is, approximately 740 b.c. 2 tn The Hebrew term translated &quot;sovereign master&quot; here and in vv. 8, 11 is אֲדֹנָי (&apos;adonay).

3 tn Hebrew שָׂרָף (saraf, &quot;seraph&quot;) literally means &quot;burning one,&quot; perhaps suggesting that these creatures had a fiery appearance (cf. TEV, CEV &quot;flaming creatures&quot;; NCV &quot;heavenly creatures of fire&quot;). Elsewhere in the OT the word &quot;seraph&quot; refers to poisonous snakes (Num 21:6; Deut 8:15; Isa 14:29; 30:6). Perhaps they were called &quot;burning ones&quot; because of their appearance or the effect of their venomous bites, which would cause a victim to burn up with fever. It is possible that the seraphs seen by Isaiah were at least partially serpentine in appearance. Though it might seem strange for a snake-like creature to have wings, two of the texts where &quot;seraphs&quot; are snakes describe them as &quot;flying&quot; (Isa 14:29; 30:6), perhaps referring to their darting movements. See the note at 14:29. 4 sn Some understand &quot;feet&quot; here as a euphemistic reference to the genitals.

5 tn Some have seen a reference to the Trinity in the seraphs&apos; threefold declaration, &quot;holy, holy, holy.&quot; This proposal has no linguistic or contextual basis and should be dismissed as allegorical. Hebrew sometimes uses repetition for emphasis. (See IBHS 233-34 §12.5a; and GKC 431-32 §133.k.) By repeating the word &quot;holy,&quot; the seraphs emphasize the degree of the Lord&apos;s holiness. For another example of threefold repetition for emphasis, see Ezek 21:27 (Heb. v. 32). (Perhaps Jer 22:29 provides another example.) sn Or &quot;The Lord who commands armies has absolute sovereign authority!&quot; The basic sense of the word &quot;holy&quot; is &quot;set apart from that which is commonplace, special, unique.&quot; In this context the Lord&apos;s holiness is first and foremost his transcendent sovereignty as the ruler of the world. He is &quot;set apart&quot; from the world over which he rules. Note the emphasis on the elevated position of his throne in v. 1 and his designation as &quot;the king&quot; in v. 5. At the same time his holiness encompasses his moral authority, which derives from his royal position. As king he has the right to dictate to his subjects how they are to live; indeed his very own character sets the standard for proper behavior. He is &quot;set apart&quot; from his subjects in a moral sense as well. He sets the standard; they fall short of it. 1 sn In the Hebrew text (BHS) the chapter division comes one verse later than in the English Bible; 9:1 (8:23 HT). Thus 9:2-21 in the English Bible = 9:1-20 in the Hebrew text. Beginning with 10:1 the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same. 2 tn The Hebrew text reads, &quot;Indeed there is no gloom for the one to whom there was anxiety for her.&quot; The feminine singular pronominal suffix &quot;her&quot; must refer to the land (cf. vv. 22a, 23b). So one could translate, &quot;Indeed there will be no gloom for the land which was anxious.&quot; In this case the statement introduces the positive message to follow. Some assume an emendation of לֹא (lo&apos;, &quot;no&quot;) to לוֹ (lo, &quot;to him&quot;) and of לָהּ (lah, &quot;to her&quot;) to לוֹ (lo, &quot;to him&quot;), yielding this literal reading: &quot;indeed there is gloom for him, for the one to whom there was anxiety for him.&quot; In this case the statement concludes the preceding description of judgment. 3 tn The Lord must be understood as the subject of the two verbs in this verse. 4 sn The statement probably alludes to the Assyrian conquest of Israel in ca. 734-733 b.c., when Tiglath-pileser III annexed much of Israel&apos;s territory and reduced Samaria to a puppet state. 5 tn Heb Just as in earlier times he humiliated..., [in] the latter times he has brought honor.&quot; The main verbs in vv. 1b-4 are Hebrew perfects. The prophet takes his rhetorical stance in the future age of restoration and describes future events as if they have already occurred. To capture the dramatic effect of the original text, the translation uses the English present or present perfect. 6 sn These three geographical designations may refer to provinces established by the Assyrians in 734-733 b.c. The &quot;way of the sea&quot; is the province of Dor, along the Mediterranean coast, the &quot;region beyond the Jordan&quot; is the province of Gilead in Transjordan, and &quot;Galilee of the nations&quot; (a title that alludes to how the territory had been overrun by foreigners) is the province of Megiddo located west of the Sea of Galilee. See Y. Aharoni, Land of the Bible, 374.

7 sn The darkness symbolizes judgment and its effects (see 8:22); the light represents deliverance and its effects, brought about by the emergence of a conquering Davidic king (see vv. 3-6). 8 tn Traditionally צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet) has been interpreted as a compound noun, meaning &quot;shadow of death&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NIV), but usage indicates that the word, though it sometimes refers to death, means &quot;darkness.&quot; The term should probably be repointed as an abstract noun צַלְמוּת (tsalmut). See the note at Ps 23:4.

9 sn The Lord is addressed directly in vv. 3-4. 10 tc The Hebrew consonantal text reads &quot;You multiply the nation, you do not make great the joy.&quot; The particle לֹא (lo&apos;, &quot;not&quot;) is obviously incorrect; the marginal reading has לוֹ (lo, &quot;to him&quot;). In this case, one should translate, &quot;You multiply the nation, you increase his (i.e., their) joy.&quot; However, the parallelism is tighter if one emends הַגּוֹי לוֹ (hagoy lo, &quot;the nation, to him&quot;) to הַגִּילָה (haggilah, &quot;the joy,&quot; a noun attested in Isa 65:18), which corresponds to הַשִּׂמְחָה (hasimkhah, &quot;the joy&quot;) later in the verse (H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:386). As attractive as this reading is, it has not textual evidence supporting it. The MT reading (accepting the marginal reading &quot;to him&quot; for the negative particle &quot;not&quot;) affirms that Yahweh caused the nation to grow in population and increased their joy. 11 tn Heb &quot;as they are happy.&quot; The word &quot;warriors&quot; is supplied in the translation to clarify the word picture. This last simile comes close to reality, for vv. 4-5 indicate that the people have won a great military victory over their oppressors.

1 sn The text mentions David&apos;s father Jesse, instead of the great king himself. Perhaps this is done for rhetorical reasons to suggest that a new David, not just another disappointing Davidic descendant, will arise. Other prophets call the coming ideal Davidic king &quot;David&quot; or picture him as the second coming of David, as it were. See Jer 30:9; Ezek 34:23-24; 37:24-25; Hos 3:5; and Mic 5:2 (as well as the note there). 2 tc The Hebrew text has יִפְרֶה (yifreh, &quot;will bear fruit,&quot; from פָּרָה, parah), but the ancient versions, as well as the parallelism suggest that יִפְרַח (yifrakh, &quot;will sprout&quot;, from פָּרַח, parakh) is the better reading here. See J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:276, n. 2.

3 sn Like David (1 Sam 16:13), this king will be energized by the Lord&apos;s spirit. 4 tn Heb &quot;a spirit of wisdom and understanding.&quot; The synonyms are joined here to emphasize the degree of wisdom he will possess. His wisdom will enable him to make just legal decisions (v. 3). A very similar phrase occurs in Eph 1:17. 5 tn Heb &quot;a spirit of counsel [or &quot;strategy&quot;] and strength.&quot; The construction is a hendiadys; the point is that he will have the strength/ability to execute the plans/strategies he devises. This ability will enable him to suppress oppressors and implement just policies (v. 4). 6 tn Heb &quot;a spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord.&quot; &quot;Knowledge&quot; is used here in its covenantal sense and refers to a recognition of God&apos;s authority and a willingness to submit to it. See Jer 22:16. &quot;Fear&quot; here refers to a healthy respect for God&apos;s authority which produces obedience. Taken together the two terms emphasize the single quality of loyalty to the Lord. This loyalty guarantees that he will make just legal decisions and implement just policies (vv. 4-5).

7 tn The Hebrew text reads literally, &quot;and his smelling is in the fear of the Lord.&quot; In Amos 5:21 the Hiphil of רוּחַ (ruakh, &quot;smell&quot;) carries the nuance of &quot;smell with delight, get pleasure from.&quot; There the Lord declares that he does not &quot;smell with delight&quot; (i.e., get pleasure from) Israel&apos;s religious assemblies, which probably stand by metonymy for the incense offered during these festivals. In Isa 11:3 there is no sacrificial context to suggest such a use, but it is possible that &quot;the fear of the Lord&quot; is likened to incense. This coming king will get the same kind of delight from obeying (fearing) the Lord, as a deity does in the incense offered by worshipers. Some regard such an explanation as strained in this context, and prefer to omit this line from the text as a virtual dittograph of the preceding statement. 8 tn Heb &quot;by what appears to his eyes&quot;; KJV &quot;after the sight of his eyes&quot;; NIV &quot;by what he sees with his eyes.&quot; 9 tn Heb &quot;by what is heard by his ears&quot;; NRSV &quot;by what his ears hear.&quot;

1 tn Heb &quot;Woe [to] the land of buzzing wings.&quot; On הוֹי (hoy, &quot;woe, ah&quot;) see the note on the first phrase of 1:4. sn The significance of the qualifying phrase &quot;buzzing wings&quot; is uncertain. Some suggest that the designation points to Cush as a land with many insects. Another possibility is that it refers to the swiftness with which this land&apos;s messengers travel (v. 2a); they move over the sea as swiftly as an insect flies through the air. For a discussion of the options, see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:359-60.

2 tn The precise meaning of the qualifying terms is uncertain. מְמֻשָּׁךְ (mÿmushakh) appears to be a Pual participle from the verb מָשַׁךְ (mashakh, &quot;to draw, extend&quot;). Lexicographers theorize that it here refers to people who &quot;stretch out,&quot; as it were, or are tall. See BDB 604 s.v. מָשַׁךְ, and HALOT 645-46 s.v. משׁךְ. מוֹרָט (morat) is taken as a Pual participle from מָרַט (marat), which can mean &quot;to pull out [hair],&quot; in the Qal, &quot;become bald&quot; in the Niphal, and &quot;be wiped clean&quot; in the Pual. Lexicographers theorize that the word here refers to people with bare, or smooth, skin. See BDB 598-99 s.v. מָרַט, and HALOT 634-35 s.v. מרט. These proposed meanings, which are based on etymological speculation, must be regarded as tentative. 3 tn Heb &quot;from it and onwards.&quot; HALOT 245 s.v. הָלְאָה suggests the translation &quot;far and wide.&quot; 4 tn Once more the precise meaning of the qualifying terms is uncertain. The expression קַו־קָו (qav-qav) is sometimes related to a proposed Arabic cognate and taken to mean &quot;strength&quot; (see BDB 876 II קַו). 1 sn The following message pertains to Jerusalem. The significance of referring to the city as the Valley of Vision is uncertain. Perhaps the Hinnom Valley is in view, but why it is associated with a prophetic revelatory &quot;vision&quot; is not entirely clear. Maybe the Hinnom Valley is called this because the destruction that will take place there is the focal point of this prophetic message (see v. 5). 2 tn Heb &quot;What to you, then?&quot;

3 tn Heb &quot;the boisterous town.&quot; The phrase is parallel to &quot;the noisy city&quot; in the preceding line. 4 sn Apparently they died from starvation during the siege that preceded the final conquest of the city. See J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:409.

5 tn Verse 3 reads literally, &quot;All your leaders ran away, apart from a bow they were captured, all your found ones were captured together, to a distant place they fled.&quot; J. N. Oswalt (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:403, n. 3) suggests that the lines of the verse are arranged chiastically; lines 1 and 4 go together, while lines 2 and 3 are parallel. To translate the lines in the order they appear in the Hebrew text is misleading to the English reader, who is likely unfamiliar with, or at least insensitive to, chiastic parallelism. Consequently, the translation above arranges the lines as follows: line 1 (Hebrew) = line 1 (in translation); line 2 (Hebrew) = line 4 (in translation); line 3 (Hebrew) = line 3 (in translation); line 4 (Hebrew) = line 2 (in translation). 6 tn Heb &quot;all your found ones.&quot; To achieve tighter parallelism (see &quot;your leaders&quot;) some prefer to emend the form to אַמִּיצַיִךְ (&apos;ammitsayikh, &quot;your strong ones&quot;) or to נֶאֱמָצַיִךְ (ne&apos;ematsayikh, &quot;your strengthened ones&quot;). 7 tn Heb &quot;apart from [i.e., without] a bow they were captured&quot;; cf. Some translate &quot;slippery&quot; or &quot;slithering.&quot; 4 tn The description of Leviathan should be compared with the following excerpts from Ugaritic mythological texts: (1) &quot;Was not the dragon (Ugaritic tnn, cognate with Hebrew תַנִּין [tannin, translated &quot;sea monster&quot; here]) vanquished and captured? I did destroy the wriggling (Ugaritic &apos;qltn, cognate to Hebrew עֲקַלָּתוֹן [&apos;aqallaton, translated &quot;squirming&quot; here]) serpent, the tyrant with seven heads (cf. Ps 74:14).&quot; (See CTA 3 iii 38-39.) (2) &quot;for all that you smote Leviathan the slippery (Ugaritic brh, cognate to Hebrew בָּרִחַ [bariakh, translated &quot;fast-moving&quot; here]) serpent, [and] made an end of the wriggling serpent, the tyrant with seven heads&quot; (See CTA 5 i 1-3.) sn In the Ugaritic mythological texts Leviathan is a sea creature that symbolizes the destructive water of the sea and in turn the forces of chaos that threaten the established order. Isaiah here applies imagery from Canaanite mythology to Yahweh&apos;s eschatological victory over his enemies. Elsewhere in the OT, the battle with the sea motif is applied to Yahweh&apos;s victories over the forces of chaos at creation and in history (cf. Pss 74:13-14; 77:16-20; 89:9-10; Isa 51:9-10). Yahweh&apos;s subjugation of the chaos waters is related to His kingship (cf. Pss 29:3, 10; 93:3-4). Apocalyptic literature employs the imagery as well. The beasts of Dan 7 emerge from the sea, while Rev 13 speaks of a seven-headed beast coming from the sea.

3 sn The expression this one from the east refers to the Persian conqueror Cyrus, as later texts indicate (see 44:28-45:6; 46:11; 48:14-16). 4 tn The interrogative particle is understood by ellipsis. 5 tn Heb &quot;[in] righteousness called him to his foot.&quot; 6 tn Heb &quot;he [the Lord] places before him [Cyrus] nations.&quot; 7 tn The verb יַרְדְּ (yardÿ) is an otherwise unattested Hiphil form from רָדָה (radah, &quot;rule&quot;). The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has יוֹרִד (yorid), which appears to be a Hiphil form from יָרַד (yarad, &quot;go down&quot;). Others suggest reading יָרֹד (yarod), a Qal form from רָדַד (radad, &quot;beat down&quot;). 8 sn The point is that they are powerless before Cyrus&apos; military power and scatter before him.

1 tn Or &quot;islands&quot; (NASB, NIV); NLT &quot;in far-off lands.&quot; sn The Lord&apos;s special servant, introduced in chap. 42, speaks here of his commission. 2 tn Heb &quot;called me from the womb.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;from the inner parts of my mother he mentioned my name.&quot;

4 tn Or perhaps, &quot;polished&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV); NASB &quot;a select arrow.&quot; 5 sn The figurative language emphasizes the servant&apos;s importance as the Lord&apos;s effective instrument. The servant&apos;s mouth, which stands metonymically for his words, is compared to a sharp sword because he will be an effective spokesman on God&apos;s behalf (see 50:4). The Lord holds his hand on the servant, ready to draw and use him at the appropriate time. The servant is like a sharpened arrow reserved in a quiver for just the right moment.

6 sn This verse identifies the servant as Israel. This seems to refer to the exiled nation (cf. 41:8-9; 44:1-2, 21; 45:4; 48:20), but in vv. 5-6 this servant says he has been commissioned to reconcile Israel to God, so he must be distinct from the exiled nation. This servant is an ideal &quot;Israel&quot; who, like Moses of old, mediates a covenant for the nation (see v. 8), leads them out of bondage (v. 9a), and carries out God&apos;s original plan for Israel by positively impacting the pagan nations (see v. 6b). By living according to God&apos;s law, Israel was to be a model of God&apos;s standards of justice to the surrounding nations (Deut 4:6-8). The sinful nation failed, but the servant, the ideal &quot;Israel,&quot; will succeed by establishing justice throughout the earth.

1 sn The Lord challenges the exiles (Zion&apos;s children) to bring incriminating evidence against him. The rhetorical questions imply that Israel accused the Lord of divorcing his wife (Zion) and selling his children (the Israelites) into slavery to pay off a debt. 2 sn The Lord admits that he did sell the Israelites, but it was because of their sins, not because of some debt he owed. If he had sold them to a creditor, they ought to be able to point him out, but the preceding rhetorical question implies they would not be able to do so. 3 sn The Lord admits he did divorce Zion, but that too was the result of the nation&apos;s sins. The force of the earlier rhetorical question comes into clearer focus now. The question does not imply that a certificate does not exist and that no divorce occurred. Rather, the question asks for the certificate to be produced so the accuser can see the reason for the divorce in black and white. The Lord did not put Zion away arbitrarily.

4 sn The present tense translation of the verbs assumes that the Lord is questioning why Israel does not attempt to counter his arguments. Another possibility is to take the verbs as referring to past events: &quot;Why did no one meet me when I came? Why did no one answer when I called?&quot; In this case the Lord might be asking why Israel rejected his calls to repent and his offer to deliver them. 5 tn Heb &quot;short&quot; (so NAB, NASB, NIV). 6 tn Or &quot;ransom&quot; (NAB, NASB, NIV). 7 tn Heb &quot;with my rebuke.&quot; 8 tn Heb &quot;the fish stink from lack of water and die from thirst.&quot;

1 tn The perfect has a hypothetical force in this rhetorical question. For another example, see Gen 21:7. 2 sn The speaker shifts here from God to an unidentified group (note the first person plural pronouns throughout vv. 1-6). The content of the speech suggests that the prophet speaks here as representative of the sinful nation Israel. The group acknowledges its sin and recognizes that the servant suffered on their behalf. 3 tn The first half of v. 1 is traditionally translated, &quot;Who has believed our report?&quot; or &quot;Who has believed our message?&quot; as if the group speaking is lamenting that no one will believe what they have to say. But that doesn&apos;t seem to be the point in this context. Here the group speaking does not cast itself in the role of a preacher or evangelist. No, they are repentant sinners, who finally see the light. The phrase &quot;our report&quot; can mean (1) the report which we deliver, or (2) the report which was delivered to us. The latter fits better here, where the report is most naturally taken as the announcement that has just been made in 52:13-15. 4 tn Heb &quot;to whom&quot; (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV). 5 tn Heb &quot;the arm of the Lord.&quot; The &quot;arm of the Lord&quot; is a metaphor of military power; it pictures the Lord as a warrior who bares his arm, takes up his weapon, and crushes his enemies (cf. 51:9-10; 63:5-6). But Israel had not seen the Lord&apos;s military power at work in the servant.

6 tn Heb &quot;before him.&quot; Some suggest an emendation to &quot;before us.&quot; If the third singular suffix of the Hebrew text is retained, it probably refers to the Lord (see v. 1b). For a defense of this reading, see R. Whybray, Isaiah 40-66 (NCBC), 173-74. 7 sn The metaphor in this verse suggests insignificance. 8 tn Heb &quot;that we might see him.&quot; The vav conjunctive prefixed to the imperfect introduces a result clause here. See GKC 504-5 §166.a. 9 tn Heb &quot;that we should desire him.&quot; The vav conjunctive prefixed to the imperfect introduces a result clause here. See GKC 504-5 §166.a.

10 tn Heb &quot;lacking of men.&quot; If the genitive is taken as specifying (&quot;lacking with respect to men&quot;), then the idea is that he lacked company because he was rejected by people. Another option is to take the genitive as indicating genus or larger class (i.e., &quot;one lacking among men&quot;). In this case one could translate, &quot;he was a transient&quot; (cf. the use of חָדֵל [khadel] in Ps 39:5 HT [39:4 ET]). 11 tn Heb &quot;like a hiding of the face from him,&quot; i.e., &quot;like one before whom the face is hidden&quot; (see BDB 712 s.v. מַסְתֵּר). 12 sn The servant is likened to a seriously ill person who is shunned by others because of his horrible disease.

1 tn The Hebrew term הוֹי (hoy, &quot;woe, ah&quot;) was used in funeral laments and is often prefixed to judgment oracles for rhetorical effect. But here it appears to be a simple interjection, designed to grab the audience&apos;s attention. Perhaps there is a note of sorrow or pity. See BDB 223 s.v. 2 sn The statement is an oxymoron. Its ironic quality adds to its rhetorical impact. The statement reminds one of the norm (one must normally buy commodities) as it expresses the astounding offer. One might paraphrase the statement: &quot;Come and take freely what you normally have to pay for.&quot;

3 tn Heb &quot;for what is not food.&quot; 4 tn The interrogative particle and the verb &quot;spend&quot; are understood here by ellipsis (note the preceding line). 5 tn Heb &quot;your labor,&quot; which stands by metonymy for that which one earns. 6 tn The infinitive absolute follows the imperative and lends emphasis to the exhortation. 7 tn Heb &quot;good&quot; (so NASB, NIV, NRSV). 8 tn Heb &quot;Let your appetite delight in fine food.&quot; sn Nourishing, fine food here represents the blessings God freely offers. These include forgiveness, a new covenantal relationship with God, and national prominence (see vv. 3-6).

9 tn The jussive with vav (ו) conjunctive following the imperative indicates purpose/result. sn To live here refers to covenantal blessing, primarily material prosperity and national security (see vv. 4-5, 13, and Deut 30:6, 15, 19-20). 10 tn Or &quot;an eternal covenant with.&quot; 11 tn Heb &quot;the reliable expressions of loyalty of David.&quot; The syntactical relationship of חַסְדֵי (khasde, &quot;expressions of loyalty&quot;) to the preceding line is unclear. If the term is appositional to בְּרִית (bÿrit, &quot;covenant&quot;), then the Lord here transfers the promises of the Davidic covenant to the entire nation. Another option is to take חַסְדֵי (khasde) as an adverbial accusative and to translate &quot;according to the reliable covenantal promises.&quot; In this case the new covenantal arrangement proposed here is viewed as an extension or perhaps fulfillment of the Davidic promises. A third option, the one reflected in the above translation, is to take the last line as comparative. In this case the new covenant being proposed is analogous to the Davidic covenant. Verses 4-5, which compare David&apos;s international prominence to what Israel will experience, favors this view. In all three of these interpretations, &quot;David&quot; is an objective genitive; he is the recipient of covenantal promises. A fourth option would be to take David as a subjective genitive and understand the line as giving the basis for the preceding promise: &quot;Then I will make an unconditional covenantal promise to you, because of David&apos;s faithful acts of covenantal loyalty.&quot;

1 tn Heb &quot;all these.&quot; The phrase refers to the heavens and earth, mentioned in the previous verse. 2 tn Heb &quot;and all these were.&quot; Some prefer to emend וַיִּהְיוּ (vayyihyu, &quot;and they were&quot;) to וְלִי הָיוּ (vÿli hayu, &quot;and to me they were&quot;), i.e., &quot;and they belong to me.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;and to this one I look&quot; (KJV and NASB both similar). 4 tn Heb &quot;to the humble and the lowly in spirit and the one who trembles at my words.&quot;

5 tn Heb &quot;one who slaughters a bull, one who strikes down a man.&quot; Some understand a comparison here and in the following lines. In God&apos;s sight the one who sacrifices is like (i.e., regarded as) a murderer or one whose worship is ritually defiled or idolatrous. The translation above assumes that the language is not metaphorical, but descriptive of the sinners&apos; hypocritical behavior. (Note the last two lines of the verse, which suggests they are guilty of abominable practices.) On the one hand, they act pious and offer sacrifices; but at the same time they commit violent crimes against men, defile their sacrifices, and worship other gods. 6 tn Heb &quot;one who sacrifices a lamb, one who breaks a dog&apos;s neck.&quot; Some understand a comparison, but see the previous note. sn The significance of breaking a dog&apos;s neck is uncertain, though the structure of the statement when compared to the preceding and following lines suggests the action is viewed in a negative light. According to Exod 13:13 and 34:20, one was to &quot;redeem&quot; a firstborn donkey by offering a lamb; if one did not &quot;redeem&quot; the firstborn donkey in this way, then its neck must be broken. According to Deut 21:1-9 a heifer&apos;s neck was to be broken as part of the atonement ritual to purify the land from the guilt of bloodshed. It is not certain if these passages relate in any way to the action described in Isa 66:3. 7 tn Heb &quot;one who offers an offering, pig&apos;s blood.&quot; Some understand a comparison, but see the note at the end of the first line. 8 tn Heb &quot;one who offers incense as a memorial offering, one who blesses something false.&quot; Some understand a comparison, but see the note at the end of the first line. אָוֶן (&apos;aven), which has a wide variety of attested nuances, here refers metonymically to an idol. See HALOT 22 s.v. and BDB 20 s.v. 2. 9 tn Heb &quot;also they have chosen their ways.&quot; 10 tn Heb &quot;their being [or &quot;soul&quot;] takes delight in their disgusting [things].&quot;

172.content: 1 map For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4. 2 tn Heb &quot;The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, [and] Hezekiah, kings of Judah.&quot; sn Isaiah&apos;s prophetic career probably began in the final year of Uzziah&apos;s reign (ca. 740 b.c., see Isa 6:1) and extended into the later years of Hezekiah&apos;s reign, which ended in 686 b.c.

3 sn The personified heavens and earth are summoned to God&apos;s courtroom as witnesses against God&apos;s covenant people. Long before this Moses warned the people that the heavens and earth would be watching their actions (see Deut 4:26; 30:19; 31:28; 32:1). 4 tn Or &quot;sons&quot; (NAB, NASB). sn &quot;Father&quot; and &quot;son&quot; occur as common terms in ancient Near Eastern treaties and covenants, delineating the suzerain and vassal as participants in the covenant relationship. The prophet uses these terms, the reference to heavens and earth as witnesses, and allusions to deuteronomic covenant curses (1:7-9, 19-20) to set his prophecy firmly against the backdrop of Israel&apos;s covenantal relationship with Yahweh. 5 sn The normal word pair for giving birth to and raising children is יָלַד (yalad, &quot;to give birth to&quot;) and גָּדַל (gadal, &quot;to grow, raise&quot;). The pair גָּדַל and רוּם (rum, &quot;to raise up&quot;) probably occur here to highlight the fact that Yahweh made something important of Israel (cf. R. Mosis, TDOT 2:403). 6 sn Against the backdrop of Yahweh&apos;s care for his chosen people, Israel&apos;s rebellion represents abhorrent treachery. The conjunction prefixed to a nonverbal element highlights the sad contrast between Yahweh&apos;s compassionate care for His people and Israel&apos;s thankless rebellion. 7 sn To rebel carries the idea of &quot;covenant treachery.&quot; Although an act of פֶּשַׁע (pesha&apos;, &quot;rebellion&quot;) often signifies a breach of the law, the legal offense also represents a violation of an existing covenantal relationship (E. Carpenter and M. Grisanti, NIDOTTE 3:707).

8 tn Heb &quot;and the donkey the feeding trough of its owner.&quot; The verb in the first line does double duty in the parallelism. 9 tn Although both verbs have no object, the parallelism suggests that Israel fails to recognize the Lord as the one who provides for their needs. In both clauses, the placement of &quot;Israel&quot; and &quot;my people&quot; at the head of the clause focuses the reader&apos;s attention on the rebellious nation (C. van der Merwe, J. Naudé, J. Kroeze, A Biblical Hebrew Reference Grammar, 346-47).

10 sn Having summoned the witnesses and announced the Lord&apos;s accusation against Israel, Isaiah mourns the nation&apos;s impending doom. The third person references to the Lord in the second half of the verse suggest that the quotation from the Lord (cf. vv. 2-3) has concluded. 11 tn Heb &quot;Woe [to the] sinful nation.&quot; The Hebrew term הוֹי, (hoy, &quot;woe, ah&quot;) was used in funeral laments (see 1 Kgs 13:30; Jer 22:18; 34:5) and carries the connotation of death. In highly dramatic fashion the prophet acts out Israel&apos;s funeral in advance, emphasizing that their demise is inevitable if they do not repent soon. 12 tn Or &quot;sons&quot; (NASB). The prophet contrasts four terms of privilege - nation, people, offspring, children - with four terms that depict Israel&apos;s sinful condition in Isaiah&apos;s day - sinful, evil, wrong, wicked (see J. A. Motyer, The Prophecy of Isaiah, 43). 13 sn Holy One of Israel is one of Isaiah&apos;s favorite divine titles for God. It pictures the Lord as the sovereign king who rules over his covenant people and exercises moral authority over them. 14 tn Heb &quot;they are estranged backward.&quot; The LXX omits this statement, which presents syntactical problems and seems to be outside the synonymous parallelistic structure of the verse.

15 sn In vv. 5-9 Isaiah addresses the battered nation (5-8) and speaks as their representative (9). 16 tn Heb &quot;Why are you still beaten? [Why] do you continue rebellion?&quot; The rhetorical questions express the prophet&apos;s disbelief over Israel&apos;s apparent masochism and obsession with sin. The interrogative construction in the first line does double duty in the parallelism. H. Wildberger (Isaiah, 1:18) offers another alternative by translating the two statements with one question: &quot;Why do you still wish to be struck that you persist in revolt?&quot; 17 tn Heb &quot;all the head is ill&quot;; NRSV &quot;the whole head is sick&quot;; CEV &quot;Your head is badly bruised.&quot; 18 tn Heb &quot;and all the heart is faint.&quot; The &quot;heart&quot; here stands for bodily strength and energy, as suggested by the context and usage elsewhere (see Jer 8:18; Lam 1:22).

19 tn Heb &quot;there is not in it health&quot;; NAB &quot;there is no sound spot.&quot; 20 tn Heb &quot;pressed out.&quot; 21 tn Heb &quot;softened&quot; (so NASB, NRSV); NIV &quot;soothed.&quot; 22 sn This verse describes wounds like those one would receive in battle. These wounds are comprehensive and without remedy.

23 tn Heb &quot;As for your land, before you foreigners are devouring it.&quot; 24 tn Heb &quot;and [there is] devastation like an overthrow by foreigners.&quot; The comparative preposition כְּ (kÿ, &quot;like, as&quot;) has here the rhetorical nuance, &quot;in every way like.&quot; The point is that the land has all the earmarks of a destructive foreign invasion because that is what has indeed happened. One could paraphrase, &quot;it is desolate as it can only be when foreigners destroy.&quot; On this use of the preposition in general, see GKC 376 §118.x. Many also prefer to emend &quot;foreigners&quot; here to &quot;Sodom,&quot; though there is no external attestation for such a reading in the mss or ancient versions. Such an emendation finds support from the following context (vv. 9-10) and usage of the preceding noun מַהְפֵּכָה (mahpekhah, &quot;overthrow&quot;). In its five other uses, this noun is associated with the destruction of Sodom. If one accepts the emendation, then one might translate, &quot;the devastation resembles the destruction of Sodom.&quot;

25 tn Heb &quot;daughter of Zion&quot; (so KJV, NASB, NIV). The genitive is appositional, identifying precisely which daughter is in view. By picturing Zion as a daughter, the prophet emphasizes her helplessness and vulnerability before the enemy. 26 tn Heb &quot;like a city besieged.&quot; Unlike the preceding two comparisons, which are purely metaphorical, this third one identifies the reality of Israel&apos;s condition. In this case the comparative preposition, as in v. 7b, has the force, &quot;in every way like,&quot; indicating that all the earmarks of a siege are visible because that is indeed what is taking place. The verb form in MT is Qal passive participle of נָצַר (natsar, &quot;guard&quot;), but since this verb is not often used of a siege (see BDB 666 s.v. I נָצַר), some prefer to repoint the form as a Niphal participle from II צוּר (tsur, &quot;besiege&quot;). However, the latter is not attested elsewhere in the Niphal (see BDB 848 s.v. II צוּר).

27 tn Traditionally, &quot;the Lord of hosts.&quot; The title pictures God as the sovereign king who has at his disposal a multitude of attendants, messengers, and warriors to do his bidding. In some contexts, like this one, the military dimension of his rulership is highlighted. In this case, the title pictures him as one who leads armies into battle against his enemies. 28 tc The translation assumes that כִּמְעָט (kim&apos;at, &quot;quickly,&quot; literally, &quot;like a little&quot;) goes with what follows, contrary to the MT accents, which take it with what precedes. In this case, one could translate the preceding line, &quot;If the Lord who commands armies had not left us a few survivors.&quot; If כִּמְעָט goes with the preceding line (following the MT accents), this expression highlights the idea that there would only be a few survivors (H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:20; H. Zobel, TDOT 8:456). Israel would not be almost like Sodom but exactly like Sodom.

29 sn Building on the simile of v. 9, the prophet sarcastically addresses the leaders and people of Jerusalem as if they were leaders and residents of ancient Sodom and Gomorrah. The sarcasm is appropriate, for if the judgment is comparable to Sodom&apos;s, that must mean that the sin which prompted the judgment is comparable as well. 30 tn Heb &quot;to the instruction of our God.&quot; In this context, which is highly accusatory and threatening, תּוֹרָה (torah, &quot;law, instruction&quot;) does not refer to mere teaching, but to corrective teaching and rebuke.

31 tn Heb &quot;Why to me the multitude of your sacrifices?&quot; The sarcastic rhetorical question suggests that their many sacrifices are of no importance to the Lord. This phrase answers the possible objection that an Israelite could raise in response to God&apos;s indictment: &quot;But we are offering the sacrifices you commanded!&quot; sn In this section the Lord refutes a potential objection that his sinful people might offer in their defense. He has charged them with rebellion (vv. 2-3), but they might respond that they have brought him many sacrifices. So he points out that he requires social justice first and foremost, not empty ritual. 32 tn The verb שָׂבַע (sava&apos;, &quot;be satisfied, full&quot;) is often used of eating and/or drinking one&apos;s fill. See BDB 959 s.v. שָׂבַע. Here sacrifices are viewed, in typical ancient Near Eastern fashion, as food for the deity. God here declares that he has eaten and drunk, as it were, his fill. 33 sn In the chiastic structure of the verse, the verbs at the beginning and end highlight God&apos;s displeasure, while the heaping up of references to animals, fat, and blood in the middle lines hints at why God wants no more of their sacrifices. They have, as it were, piled the food on his table and he needs no more.

34 tn Heb &quot;When you come to appear before me, who requires this from your hand, trampling of my courtyards?&quot; The rhetorical question sarcastically makes the point that God does not require this parade of livestock. The verb &quot;trample&quot; probably refers to the eager worshipers and their sacrificial animals walking around in the temple area.

35 tn Or &quot;worthless&quot; (NASB, NCV, CEV); KJV, ASV &quot;vain.&quot; 36 sn Notice some of the other practices that Yahweh regards as &quot;detestable&quot;: homosexuality (Lev 18:22-30; 20:13), idolatry (Deut 7:25; 13:15), human sacrifice (Deut 12:31), eating ritually unclean animals (Deut 14:3-8), sacrificing defective animals (Deut 17:1), engaging in occult activities (Deut 18:9-14), and practicing ritual prostitution (1 Kgs 14:23). 37 tn Heb &quot;sin and assembly&quot; (these two nouns probably represent a hendiadys). The point is that their attempts at worship are unacceptable to God because the people&apos;s everyday actions in the socio-economic realm prove they have no genuine devotion to God (see vv. 16-17).

38 tn Heb &quot;I close my eyes from you.&quot; 39 sn This does not just refer to the blood of sacrificial animals, but also the blood, as it were, of their innocent victims. By depriving the poor and destitute of proper legal recourse and adequate access to the economic system, the oppressors have, for all intents and purposes, &quot;killed&quot; their victims.

40 sn Having demonstrated the people&apos;s guilt, the Lord calls them to repentance, which will involve concrete action in the socio-economic realm, not mere emotion. 41 sn This phrase refers to Israel&apos;s covenant treachery (cf. Deut 28:10; Jer 4:4; 21:12; 23:2, 22; 25:5; 26:3; 44:22; Hos 9:15; Ps 28:4). In general, the noun ַמעַלְלֵיכֶם (ma&apos;alleykhem) can simply be a reference to deeds, whether good or bad. However, Isaiah always uses it with a negative connotation (cf. 3:8, 10).

42 tn The precise meaning of this line is uncertain. The translation assumes an emendation of חָמוֹץ (khamots, &quot;oppressor [?]&quot;) to חָמוּץ (khamuts, &quot;oppressed&quot;), a passive participle from II חָמַץ (khamats, &quot;oppress&quot;; HALOT 329 s.v. II חמץ) and takes the verb II אָשַׁר (&apos;ashar) in the sense of &quot;make happy&quot; (the delocutive Piel, meaning &quot;call/pronounce happy,&quot; is metonymic here, referring to actually effecting happiness). The parallelism favors this interpretation, for the next two lines speak of positive actions on behalf of the destitute. The other option is to retain the MT pointing and translate, &quot;set right the oppressor,&quot; but the nuance &quot;set right&quot; is not clearly attested elsewhere for the verb I אשׁר. This verb does appear as a participle in Isa 3:12 and 9:16 with the meaning &quot;to lead or guide.&quot; If it can mean to &quot;lead&quot; or &quot;rebuke/redirect&quot; in this verse, the prophet could be contrasting this appeal for societal reformation (v. 17c) with a command to reorder their personal lives (v. 17a-b). J. A. Motyer (The Prophecy of Isaiah, 47) suggests that these three statements (v. 17a-c) provide &quot;the contrast between the two ends of imperfect society, the oppressor and the needy, the one inflicting and the other suffering the hurt. Isaiah looks for a transformed society wherever it needs transforming.&quot; 43 tn This word refers to a woman who has lost her husband, by death or divorce. The orphan and widow are often mentioned in the OT as epitomizing the helpless and impoverished who have been left without the necessities of life due to the loss of a family provider.

44 sn The Lord concludes his case against Israel by offering them the opportunity to be forgiven and by setting before them the alternatives of renewed blessing (as a reward for repentance) and final judgment (as punishment for persistence in sin). 45 tn Traditionally, &quot;let us reason together,&quot; but the context suggests a judicial nuance. The Lord is giving the nation its options for the future. 46 tn The imperfects must be translated as modal (indicating capability or possibility) to bring out the conditional nature of the offer. This purification will only occur if the people repent and change their ways. 47 tn The imperfects must be translated as modal (indicating capability or possibility) to bring out the conditional nature of the offer. This purification will only occur if the people repent and change their ways. 48 tn Heb &quot;though your sins are like red, they will become white like snow; though they are red like scarlet, they will be like wool.&quot; The point is not that the sins will be covered up, though still retained. The metaphorical language must be allowed some flexibility and should not be pressed into a rigid literalistic mold. The people&apos;s sins will be removed and replaced by ethical purity. The sins that are now as obvious as the color red will be washed away and the ones who are sinful will be transformed.
49 tn Heb &quot;listen&quot;; KJV &quot;obedient&quot;; NASB &quot;If you consent and obey.&quot;

50 sn The wordplay in the Hebrew draws attention to the options. The people can obey, in which case they will &quot;eat&quot; v. 19 (תֹּאכֵלוּ [to&apos;khelu], Qal active participle of אָכַל) God&apos;s blessing, or they can disobey, in which case they will be devoured (Heb &quot;eaten,&quot; תְּאֻכְּלוּ, [tÿ&apos;ukkÿlu], Qal passive/Pual of אָכַל) by God&apos;s judgment. 51 tn Heb &quot;for the mouth of the Lord has spoken.&quot; The introductory כִּי (ki) may be asseverative (as reflected in the translation) or causal/explanatory, explaining why the option chosen by the people will become reality (it is guaranteed by the divine word).

52 tn Heb &quot;How she has become a prostitute, the faithful city!&quot; The exclamatory אֵיכָה (&apos;ekhah, &quot;how!&quot;) is used several times as the beginning of a lament (see Lam 1:1; 2;1; 4:1-2). Unlike a number of other OT passages that link references to Israel&apos;s harlotry to idolatry, Isaiah here makes the connection with social and moral violations. 53 tn Heb &quot;filled with.&quot; 54 tn Or &quot;assassins.&quot; This refers to the oppressive rich and/or their henchmen. R. Ortlund (Whoredom, 78) posits that it serves as a synecdoche for all varieties of criminals, the worst being mentioned to imply all lesser ones. Since Isaiah often addressed his strongest rebuke to the rulers and leaders of Israel, he may have in mind the officials who bore the responsibility to uphold justice and righteousness.

55 tn The pronoun is feminine singular; personified Jerusalem (see v. 21) is addressed. 56 tn Or &quot;dross.&quot; The word refers to the scum or impurites floating on the top of melted metal. 57 sn The metaphors of silver becoming impure and beer being watered down picture the moral and ethical degeneration that had occurred in Jerusalem.

58 tn Or &quot;stubborn&quot;; CEV &quot;have rejected me.&quot; 59 tn Heb &quot;and companions of&quot; (so KJV, NASB); CEV &quot;friends of crooks.&quot; 60 tn Heb &quot;pursue&quot;; NIV &quot;chase after gifts.&quot; 61 sn Isaiah may have chosen the word for gifts (שַׁלְמוֹנִים, shalmonim; a hapax legomena here), as a sarcastic pun on what these rulers should have been doing. Instead of attending to peace and wholeness (שָׁלוֹם, shalom), they sought after payoffs (שַׁלְמוֹנִים). 62 sn See the note at v. 17. 63 sn The rich oppressors referred to in Isaiah and the other eighth century prophets were not rich capitalists in the modern sense of the word. They were members of the royal military and judicial bureaucracies in Israel and Judah. As these bureaucracies grew, they acquired more and more land and gradually commandeered the economy and legal system. At various administrative levels bribery and graft become commonplace. The common people outside the urban administrative centers were vulnerable to exploitation in such a system, especially those, like widows and orphans, who had lost their family provider through death. Through confiscatory taxation, conscription, excessive interest rates, and other oppressive governmental measures and policies, they were gradually disenfranchised and lost their landed property, and with it, their rights as citizens. The socio-economic equilibrium envisioned in the law of Moses was radically disturbed.

64 tn Heb &quot;the master, the Lord who commands armies [traditionally, the Lord of hosts].&quot; On the title &quot;the Lord who commands armies,&quot; see the note at v. 9. 65 tn Heb &quot;the powerful [one] of Israel.&quot; 66 tn Heb &quot;console myself&quot; (i.e., by getting revenge); NRSV &quot;pour out my wrath on.&quot; 67 sn The Lord here identifies with the oppressed and comes as their defender and vindicator.

68 tn Heb &quot;turn my hand against you.&quot; The second person pronouns in vv. 25-26 are feminine singular. Personified Jerusalem is addressed. The idiom &quot;turn the hand against&quot; has the nuance of &quot;strike with the hand, attack,&quot; in Ps 81:15 HT (81:14 ET); Ezek 38:12; Am 1:8; Zech 13:7. In Jer 6:9 it is used of gleaning grapes. 69 tn Heb &quot;I will purify your dross as [with] flux.&quot; &quot;Flux&quot; refers here to minerals added to the metals in a furnace to prevent oxides from forming. For this interpretation of II בֹּר (bor), see HALOT 153 s.v. II בֹּר and 750 s.v. סִיג. 70 sn The metaphor comes from metallurgy; slag is the substance left over after the metallic ore has been refined.

71 tn Heb &quot;I will restore your judges as in the beginning; and your counselors as in the beginning.&quot; In this context, where social injustice and legal corruption are denounced (see v. 23), the &quot;judges&quot; are probably government officials responsible for making legal decisions, while the &quot;advisers&quot; are probably officials who helped the king establish policies. Both offices are also mentioned in 3:2.

72 sn The third person reference to the Lord in v. 28 indicates that the prophet is again (see vv. 21-24a) speaking. Since v. 27 is connected to v. 28 by a conjunction, it is likely that the prophet&apos;s words begin with v. 27. 73 tn Heb &quot;Zion will be ransomed with justice.&quot; Both cola in this verse end with similar terms: justice and righteousness (and both are preceded by a בְּ [bet] preposition). At issue is whether these virtues describe the means or result of the deliverance and whether they delineate God&apos;s justice/righteousness or that of the covenant people. If the righteousness of Israelite returnees is in view, the point seems to be that the reestablishment of Zion as a center of justice (God&apos;s people living in conformity with God&apos;s demand for equity and justice) will deliver the city from its past humiliation and restore it to a place of prominence (see 2:2-4; cf. E. Kissane, Isaiah, 1:19). Most scholars conclude that &quot;righteousness and &quot;justice&quot; refers to God alone (J. Ridderbos, Isaiah [BSC], 50; J. Watts, Isaiah [WBC], 1:25; E. J. Young, Isaiah [NICOT], 1:89; cf. NLT, TEV) or serves as a double reference to both divine and human justice and righteousness (J. A. Motyer, The Prophecy of Isaiah, 51; J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah [NICOT], 1:10; H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:72). If it refers to both sides of the coin, these terms highlight the objective divine work of redemption and the subjective human response of penitence (Motyer, 51). 74 tc The Hebrew text has, &quot;her repentant ones/returnees with righteousness.&quot; The form שָׁבֶיהָ (shaveha, &quot;her repentant ones&quot;), as pointed in MT, is a masculine plural Qal participle from שׁוּב (shuv, &quot;return&quot;). Used substantivally, it refers to the &quot;returning (i.e., repentant) ones.&quot; It is possible that the parallel line (with its allusion to being freed by a ransom payment) suggests that the form be repointed to שִׁבְיָהּ (shivyah, &quot;her captivity&quot;), a reading that has support from the LXX. Some slightly emend the form to read וְשָׁבָה (vÿshavah, &quot;and will return&quot;). According to this view, the verb from the first line applies to the second line as well with the following translation as a result: &quot;she will be released when fairness is restored.&quot; Regardless, it makes best sense in the context to regard this as a reference to repentant Israelites returning to the land of promise. This understanding provides a better contrast with the rebels and sinners in 1:28.
75 tn Heb &quot;and [there will be] a shattering of rebels and sinners together.&quot;

76 tc The Hebrew text (and the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa) has the third person here, though a few Hebrew mss (and Targums) read the second person, which is certainly more consistent with the following context. The third person form is the more difficult reading and probably original. This disagreement in person has caused some to emend the first verb (3rd plural) to a 2nd plural form (followed by most English translations). The BHS textual apparatus suggests that the 2nd plural form be read even though there is only sparse textual evidence. LXX, Syriac, and the Vulgate change all the 2nd person verbs in 1:29-31 to 3rd person verbs. It is likely that the change to a 2nd person form represents an attempt at syntactical harmonization (J. de Waard, Isaiah, 10). The abrupt change from 3rd person to 2nd person may have been intentional for rhetorical impact (GKC 462 §144.p). The rapid change from exclamation (they did!) to reproach (you desired!) might be regarded as a rhetorical figure focusing attention on the addressees and their conditions (de Waard, 10; E. König, Stilistik, Rhetorik, Poetik, 239). This use of the 3rd person could also be understood as an impersonal third person: &quot;one will be ashamed&quot; (de Waard, 10). In v. 29 the prophet continues his description of the sinners (v. 28), but then suddenly makes a transition to direct address (switching from 3rd to 2nd person) in the middle of his sentence. 77 tn The second person pronouns in vv. 29-30 are masculine plural, indicating that the rebellious sinners (v. 28) are addressed. 78 tn Or &quot;gardens&quot; (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV); NAB &quot;groves.&quot;
79 tn Or &quot;a garden&quot; (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV).
80 tn Heb &quot;will become&quot; (so NASB, NIV).

3 tn Heb &quot;in the end of the days.&quot; This phrase may refer generally to the future, or more technically to the final period of history. See BDB 31 s.v. ַאחֲרִית. The verse begins with a verb that functions as a &quot;discourse particle&quot; and is not translated. In numerous places throughout the OT, the &quot;to be&quot; verb with a prefixed conjunction (וְהָיָה [vÿhayah] and וַיְהִי [vayÿhi]) occurs in this fashion to introduce a circumstantial clause and does not require translation. 4 tn Or &quot;be established&quot; (KJV, NIV, NRSV). 5 tn Heb &quot;as the chief of the mountains, and will be lifted up above the hills.&quot; The image of Mount Zion being elevated above other mountains and hills pictures the prominence it will attain in the future.

6 tn The prefixed verb form with simple vav (ו) introduces a purpose/result clause after the preceding prefixed verb form (probably to be taken as a cohortative; see IBHS 650 §39.2.2a). 7 tn Heb &quot;his ways.&quot; In this context God&apos;s &quot;ways&quot; are the standards of moral conduct he decrees that people should live by. 8 tn The cohortative with vav (ו) after the prefixed verb form indicates the ultimate purpose/goal of their action. 9 tn Heb &quot;walk in his ways.&quot; 10 tn Heb &quot;for out of Zion will go instruction.&quot; 11 tn Heb &quot;the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.&quot;

1 tn Or &quot;in that day&quot; (ASV). sn The seven to one ratio emphasizes the great disparity that will exist in the population due to the death of so many men in battle. 2 tn Heb &quot;eat&quot; (so NASB, NIV, NRSV); CEV &quot;buy.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;wear&quot; (so NASB, NRSV); NCV &quot;make.&quot; 4 tn Heb &quot;only let your name be called over us.&quot; The Hebrew idiom &quot;call the name over&quot; indicates ownership. See 2 Sam 12:28, and BDB 896 s.v. I ָקרָא Niph. 2.d.(4). The language reflects the cultural reality of ancient Israel, where women were legally the property of their husbands. 5 sn This refers to the humiliation of being unmarried and childless. The women&apos;s words reflect the cultural standards of ancient Israel, where a woman&apos;s primary duties were to be a wife and mother.

6 tn Or &quot;in that day&quot; (KJV). 7 tn Heb &quot;and the vegetation of the Lord will become beauty and honor.&quot; Many English versions understand the phrase צֶמַח יְהוָה (tsemakh yÿhvah) as a messianic reference and render it, &quot;the Branch of the Lord&quot; (so KJV, NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT, and others). Though צֶמַח (tsemakh) is used by later prophets of a royal descendant (Jer 23;5; 33:15; Zech 3:8; 6:12), those passages contain clear contextual indicators that a human ruler is in view and that the word is being used in a metaphorical way of offspring. However, in Isa 4:2 there are no such contextual indicators. To the contrary, in the parallel structure of the verse צֶמַח יְהוָה corresponds to &quot;produce of the land,&quot; a phrase that refers elsewhere exclusively to literal agricultural produce (see Num 13:20, 26; Deut 1:25). In the majority of its uses צֶמַח refers to literal crops or vegetation (in Ps 65:10 the Lord is the source of this vegetation). A reference to the Lord restoring crops would make excellent sense in Isa 4 and the prophets frequently included this theme in their visions of the future age (see Isa 30:23-24; 32:20; Jer 31:12; Ezek 34:26-29; and Amos 9:13-14). 8 tn Heb &quot;and the fruit of the land will become pride and beauty for the remnant of Israel.&quot;

9 tn The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on &quot;in the future&quot; in 2:2. 10 map For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4. 11 tn Or &quot;set apart,&quot; cf. CEV &quot;special.&quot; 12 tn Heb &quot;all who are written down for life in Jerusalem.&quot; A city register is envisioned; everyone whose name appears on the roll will be spared. This group comprises the remnant of the city referred to earlier in the verse.

1 tn It is uncertain who is speaking here. Possibly the prophet, taking the role of best man, composes a love song for his friend on the occasion of his wedding. If so, יָדִיד (yadid) should be translated &quot;my friend.&quot; The present translation assumes that Israel is singing to the Lord. The word דוֹד (dod, &quot;lover&quot;) used in the second line is frequently used by the woman in the Song of Solomon to describe her lover. 2 sn Israel, viewing herself as the Lord&apos;s lover, refers to herself as his vineyard. The metaphor has sexual connotations, for it pictures her capacity to satisfy his appetite and to produce children. See Song 8:12. 3 tn Heb &quot;on a horn, a son of oil.&quot; Apparently קֶרֶן (qeren, &quot;horn&quot;) here refers to the horn-shaped peak of a hill (BDB 902 s.v.) or to a mountain spur, i.e., a ridge that extends laterally from a mountain (HALOT 1145 s.v. קֶרֶן; H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:180). The expression &quot;son of oil&quot; pictures this hill as one capable of producing olive trees. Isaiah&apos;s choice of קֶרֶן, a rare word for hill, may have been driven by paronomastic concerns, i.e., because קֶרֶן sounds like כֶּרֶם (kerem, &quot;vineyard&quot;).

For another example of threefold repetition for emphasis, see Ezek 21:27 (Heb. v. 32). (Perhaps Jer 22:29 provides another example.) sn Or &quot;The Lord who commands armies has absolute sovereign authority!&quot; The basic sense of the word &quot;holy&quot; is &quot;set apart from that which is commonplace, special, unique.&quot; In this context the Lord&apos;s holiness is first and foremost his transcendent sovereignty as the ruler of the world. 1 sn In the Hebrew text (BHS) the chapter division comes one verse later than in the English Bible; 9:1 (8:23 HT). Thus 9:2-21 in the English Bible = 9:1-20 in the Hebrew text. Beginning with 10:1 the verse numbers in the English Bible and the Hebrew Bible are again the same. 2 tn The Hebrew text reads, &quot;Indeed there is no gloom for the one to whom there was anxiety for her.&quot; The feminine singular pronominal suffix &quot;her&quot; must refer to the land (cf. vv. 22a, 23b). So one could translate, &quot;Indeed there will be no gloom for the land which was anxious.&quot; In this case the statement introduces the positive message to follow. Some assume an emendation of לֹא (lo&apos;, &quot;no&quot;) to לוֹ (lo, &quot;to him&quot;) and of לָהּ (lah, &quot;to her&quot;) to לוֹ (lo, &quot;to him&quot;), yielding this literal reading: &quot;indeed there is gloom for him, for the one to whom there was anxiety for him.&quot; In this case the statement concludes the preceding description of judgment. 3 tn The Lord must be understood as the subject of the two verbs in this verse. 4 sn The statement probably alludes to the Assyrian conquest of Israel in ca. 734-733 b.c., when Tiglath-pileser III annexed much of Israel&apos;s territory and reduced Samaria to a puppet state. 5 tn Heb Just as in earlier times he humiliated..., [in] the latter times he has brought honor.&quot; The main verbs in vv. 1b-4 are Hebrew perfects. The prophet takes his rhetorical stance in the future age of restoration and describes future events as if they have already occurred. To capture the dramatic effect of the original text, the translation uses the English present or present perfect. 6 sn These three geographical designations may refer to provinces established by the Assyrians in 734-733 b.c. The &quot;way of the sea&quot; is the province of Dor, along the Mediterranean coast, the &quot;region beyond the Jordan&quot; is the province of Gilead in Transjordan, and &quot;Galilee of the nations&quot; (a title that alludes to how the territory had been overrun by foreigners) is the province of Megiddo located west of the Sea of Galilee. See Y. Aharoni, Land of the Bible, 374.

7 sn The darkness symbolizes judgment and its effects (see 8:22); the light represents deliverance and its effects, brought about by the emergence of a conquering Davidic king (see vv. 3-6). 8 tn Traditionally צַלְמָוֶת (tsalmavet) has been interpreted as a compound noun, meaning &quot;shadow of death&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NIV), but usage indicates that the word, though it sometimes refers to death, means &quot;darkness.&quot; The term should probably be repointed as an abstract noun צַלְמוּת (tsalmut). See the note at Ps 23:4.

9 sn The Lord is addressed directly in vv. 3-4. 10 tc The Hebrew consonantal text reads &quot;You multiply the nation, you do not make great the joy.&quot; The particle לֹא (lo&apos;, &quot;not&quot;) is obviously incorrect; the marginal reading has לוֹ (lo, &quot;to him&quot;). In this case, one should translate, &quot;You multiply the nation, you increase his (i.e., their) joy.&quot; However, the parallelism is tighter if one emends הַגּוֹי לוֹ (hagoy lo, &quot;the nation, to him&quot;) to הַגִּילָה (haggilah, &quot;the joy,&quot; a noun attested in Isa 65:18), which corresponds to הַשִּׂמְחָה (hasimkhah, &quot;the joy&quot;) later in the verse (H. Wildberger, Isaiah, 1:386). As attractive as this reading is, it has not textual evidence supporting it. The MT reading (accepting the marginal reading &quot;to him&quot; for the negative particle &quot;not&quot;) affirms that Yahweh caused the nation to grow in population and increased their joy. 11 tn Heb &quot;as they are happy.&quot; The word &quot;warriors&quot; is supplied in the translation to clarify the word picture. This last simile comes close to reality, for vv. 4-5 indicate that the people have won a great military victory over their oppressors.

See Jer 30:9; Ezek 34:23-24; 37:24-25; Hos 3:5; and Mic 5:2 (as well as the note there). 2 tc The Hebrew text has יִפְרֶה (yifreh, &quot;will bear fruit,&quot; from פָּרָה, parah), but the ancient versions, as well as the parallelism suggest that יִפְרַח (yifrakh, &quot;will sprout&quot;, from פָּרַח, parakh) is the better reading here. See J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:276, n. 2.

3 sn Like David (1 Sam 16:13), this king will be energized by the Lord&apos;s spirit. 4 tn Heb &quot;a spirit of wisdom and understanding.&quot; The synonyms are joined here to emphasize the degree of wisdom he will possess. His wisdom will enable him to make just legal decisions (v. 3). A very similar phrase occurs in Eph 1:17. 5 tn Heb &quot;a spirit of counsel [or &quot;strategy&quot;] and strength.&quot; The construction is a hendiadys; the point is that he will have the strength/ability to execute the plans/strategies he devises. This ability will enable him to suppress oppressors and implement just policies (v. 4). 6 tn Heb &quot;a spirit of knowledge and fear of the Lord.&quot; &quot;Knowledge&quot; is used here in its covenantal sense and refers to a recognition of God&apos;s authority and a willingness to submit to it. See Jer 22:16. &quot;Fear&quot; here refers to a healthy respect for God&apos;s authority which produces obedience. Taken together the two terms emphasize the single quality of loyalty to the Lord. This loyalty guarantees that he will make just legal decisions and implement just policies (vv. 4-5).

7 tn The Hebrew text reads literally, &quot;and his smelling is in the fear of the Lord.&quot; In Amos 5:21 the Hiphil of רוּחַ (ruakh, &quot;smell&quot;) carries the nuance of &quot;smell with delight, get pleasure from.&quot; There the Lord declares that he does not &quot;smell with delight&quot; (i.e., get pleasure from) Israel&apos;s religious assemblies, which probably stand by metonymy for the incense offered during these festivals. In Isa 11:3 there is no sacrificial context to suggest such a use, but it is possible that &quot;the fear of the Lord&quot; is likened to incense. This coming king will get the same kind of delight from obeying (fearing) the Lord, as a deity does in the incense offered by worshipers. Some regard such an explanation as strained in this context, and prefer to omit this line from the text as a virtual dittograph of the preceding statement. 8 tn Heb &quot;by what appears to his eyes&quot;; KJV &quot;after the sight of his eyes&quot;; NIV &quot;by what he sees with his eyes.&quot; 9 tn Heb &quot;by what is heard by his ears&quot;; NRSV &quot;by what his ears hear.&quot;

1 tn Heb &quot;Woe [to] the land of buzzing wings.&quot; On הוֹי (hoy, &quot;woe, ah&quot;) see the note on the first phrase of 1:4. sn The significance of the qualifying phrase &quot;buzzing wings&quot; is uncertain. Some suggest that the designation points to Cush as a land with many insects. Another possibility is that it refers to the swiftness with which this land&apos;s messengers travel (v. 2a); they move over the sea as swiftly as an insect flies through the air. For a discussion of the options, see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:359-60.

2 tn The precise meaning of the qualifying terms is uncertain. מְמֻשָּׁךְ (mÿmushakh) appears to be a Pual participle from the verb מָשַׁךְ (mashakh, &quot;to draw, extend&quot;). Lexicographers theorize that it here refers to people who &quot;stretch out,&quot; as it were, or are tall. See BDB 604 s.v. מָשַׁךְ, and HALOT 645-46 s.v. משׁךְ. מוֹרָט (morat) is taken as a Pual participle from מָרַט (marat), which can mean &quot;to pull out [hair],&quot; in the Qal, &quot;become bald&quot; in the Niphal, and &quot;be wiped clean&quot; in the Pual. Lexicographers theorize that the word here refers to people with bare, or smooth, skin. See BDB 598-99 s.v. מָרַט, and HALOT 634-35 s.v. מרט. These proposed meanings, which are based on etymological speculation, must be regarded as tentative. 3 tn Heb &quot;from it and onwards.&quot; HALOT 245 s.v. הָלְאָה suggests the translation &quot;far and wide.&quot; 4 tn Once more the precise meaning of the qualifying terms is uncertain. The expression קַו־קָו (qav-qav) is sometimes related to a proposed Arabic cognate and taken to mean &quot;strength&quot; (see BDB 876 II קַו). Others, on the basis of Isa 28:10, 13, understand the form as gibberish (literally, &quot;kav, kav&quot;) and take it to be a reference to this nation&apos;s strange, unknown language. The form מְבוּסָה (mÿvusah) appears to be derived from בּוּס (bus, &quot;to trample&quot;), so lexicographers suggest the meaning &quot;trampling&quot; or &quot;subjugation,&quot; i.e., a nation that subdues others. See BDB 101 s.v. בּוּס and HALOT 541 s.v. מְבוּסָה. These proposals, which are based on etymological speculation, must be regarded as tentative. 5 tn The precise meaning of the verb בָּזָא (baza&apos;), which occurs only in this oracle (see also v. 7) in the OT, is uncertain. BDB 102 s.v. suggests &quot;divide&quot; on the basis of alleged Aramaic and Arabic cognates; HALOT 117 s.v., citing an alleged Arabic cognate, suggests &quot;wash away.&quot;

1 sn The following message pertains to Jerusalem. The significance of referring to the city as the Valley of Vision is uncertain. Perhaps the Hinnom Valley is in view, but why it is associated with a prophetic revelatory &quot;vision&quot; is not entirely clear. 3 tn Heb &quot;the boisterous town.&quot; The phrase is parallel to &quot;the noisy city&quot; in the preceding line. 4 sn Apparently they died from starvation during the siege that preceded the final conquest of the city. See J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah (NICOT), 1:409.

5 tn Verse 3 reads literally, &quot;All your leaders ran away, apart from a bow they were captured, all your found ones were captured together, to a distant place they fled.&quot; J. N. Oswalt (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:403, n. 3) suggests that the lines of the verse are arranged chiastically; lines 1 and 4 go together, while lines 2 and 3 are parallel. To translate the lines in the order they appear in the Hebrew text is misleading to the English reader, who is likely unfamiliar with, or at least insensitive to, chiastic parallelism. Consequently, the translation above arranges the lines as follows: line 1 (Hebrew) = line 1 (in translation); line 2 (Hebrew) = line 4 (in translation); line 3 (Hebrew) = line 3 (in translation); line 4 (Hebrew) = line 2 (in translation). 6 tn Heb &quot;all your found ones.&quot; To achieve tighter parallelism (see &quot;your leaders&quot;) some prefer to emend the form to אַמִּיצַיִךְ (&apos;ammitsayikh, &quot;your strong ones&quot;) or to נֶאֱמָצַיִךְ (ne&apos;ematsayikh, &quot;your strengthened ones&quot;). 7 tn Heb &quot;apart from [i.e., without] a bow they were captured&quot;; cf. NAB, NRSV &quot;cruel&quot;; KJV &quot;sore&quot;; NLT &quot;terrible.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;fleeing&quot; (so NAB, NASB, NRSV). Some translate &quot;slippery&quot; or &quot;slithering.&quot; 4 tn The description of Leviathan should be compared with the following excerpts from Ugaritic mythological texts: (1) &quot;Was not the dragon (Ugaritic tnn, cognate with Hebrew תַנִּין [tannin, translated &quot;sea monster&quot; here]) vanquished and captured? I did destroy the wriggling (Ugaritic &apos;qltn, cognate to Hebrew עֲקַלָּתוֹן [&apos;aqallaton, translated &quot;squirming&quot; here]) serpent, the tyrant with seven heads (cf. Ps 74:14).&quot; (See CTA 3 iii 38-39.) (2) &quot;for all that you smote Leviathan the slippery (Ugaritic brh, cognate to Hebrew בָּרִחַ [bariakh, translated &quot;fast-moving&quot; here]) serpent, [and] made an end of the wriggling serpent, the tyrant with seven heads&quot; (See CTA 5 i 1-3.) sn In the Ugaritic mythological texts Leviathan is a sea creature that symbolizes the destructive water of the sea and in turn the forces of chaos that threaten the established order. Isaiah here applies imagery from Canaanite mythology to Yahweh&apos;s eschatological victory over his enemies. Elsewhere in the OT, the battle with the sea motif is applied to Yahweh&apos;s victories over the forces of chaos at creation and in history (cf. Pss 74:13-14; 77:16-20; 89:9-10; Isa 51:9-10). Yahweh&apos;s subjugation of the chaos waters is related to His kingship (cf. Pss 29:3, 10; 93:3-4). Apocalyptic literature employs the imagery as well. The beasts of Dan 7 emerge from the sea, while Rev 13 speaks of a seven-headed beast coming from the sea.

The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has יוֹרִד (yorid), which appears to be a Hiphil form from יָרַד (yarad, &quot;go down&quot;). Others suggest reading יָרֹד (yarod), a Qal form from רָדַד (radad, &quot;beat down&quot;). 8 sn The point is that they are powerless before Cyrus&apos; military power and scatter before him.

1 tn Or &quot;islands&quot; (NASB, NIV); NLT &quot;in far-off lands.&quot; sn The Lord&apos;s special servant, introduced in chap. 42, speaks here of his commission. 2 tn Heb &quot;called me from the womb.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;from the inner parts of my mother he mentioned my name.&quot;

4 tn Or perhaps, &quot;polished&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NAB, NIV, NRSV); NASB &quot;a select arrow.&quot; 5 sn The figurative language emphasizes the servant&apos;s importance as the Lord&apos;s effective instrument. The servant&apos;s mouth, which stands metonymically for his words, is compared to a sharp sword because he will be an effective spokesman on God&apos;s behalf (see 50:4). The Lord holds his hand on the servant, ready to draw and use him at the appropriate time. The servant is like a sharpened arrow reserved in a quiver for just the right moment.

6 sn This verse identifies the servant as Israel. This seems to refer to the exiled nation (cf. 41:8-9; 44:1-2, 21; 45:4; 48:20), but in vv. 5-6 this servant says he has been commissioned to reconcile Israel to God, so he must be distinct from the exiled nation. This servant is an ideal &quot;Israel&quot; who, like Moses of old, mediates a covenant for the nation (see v. 8), leads them out of bondage (v. 9a), and carries out God&apos;s original plan for Israel by positively impacting the pagan nations (see v. 6b). By living according to God&apos;s law, Israel was to be a model of God&apos;s standards of justice to the surrounding nations (Deut 4:6-8). The sinful nation failed, but the servant, the ideal &quot;Israel,&quot; will succeed by establishing justice throughout the earth.

1 sn The Lord challenges the exiles (Zion&apos;s children) to bring incriminating evidence against him. The rhetorical questions imply that Israel accused the Lord of divorcing his wife (Zion) and selling his children (the Israelites) into slavery to pay off a debt. 2 sn The Lord admits that he did sell the Israelites, but it was because of their sins, not because of some debt he owed. 1 tn The perfect has a hypothetical force in this rhetorical question. For another example, see Gen 21:7. 2 sn The speaker shifts here from God to an unidentified group (note the first person plural pronouns throughout vv. 1-6). The content of the speech suggests that the prophet speaks here as representative of the sinful nation Israel. The group acknowledges its sin and recognizes that the servant suffered on their behalf. 3 tn The first half of v. 1 is traditionally translated, &quot;Who has believed our report?&quot; or &quot;Who has believed our message?&quot; as if the group speaking is lamenting that no one will believe what they have to say. But that doesn&apos;t seem to be the point in this context. Here the group speaking does not cast itself in the role of a preacher or evangelist. No, they are repentant sinners, who finally see the light. The phrase &quot;our report&quot; can mean (1) the report which we deliver, or (2) the report which was delivered to us. The latter fits better here, where the report is most naturally taken as the announcement that has just been made in 52:13-15. 4 tn Heb &quot;to whom&quot; (so KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV). 5 tn Heb &quot;the arm of the Lord.&quot; The &quot;arm of the Lord&quot; is a metaphor of military power; it pictures the Lord as a warrior who bares his arm, takes up his weapon, and crushes his enemies (cf. 51:9-10; 63:5-6). But Israel had not seen the Lord&apos;s military power at work in the servant.

6 tn Heb &quot;before him.&quot; Some suggest an emendation to &quot;before us.&quot; If the third singular suffix of the Hebrew text is retained, it probably refers to the Lord (see v. 1b). For a defense of this reading, see R. Whybray, Isaiah 40-66 (NCBC), 173-74. 7 sn The metaphor in this verse suggests insignificance. 8 tn Heb &quot;that we might see him.&quot; The vav conjunctive prefixed to the imperfect introduces a result clause here. See GKC 504-5 §166.a. 9 tn Heb &quot;that we should desire him.&quot; The vav conjunctive prefixed to the imperfect introduces a result clause here. See GKC 504-5 §166.a.

10 tn Heb &quot;lacking of men.&quot; If the genitive is taken as specifying (&quot;lacking with respect to men&quot;), then the idea is that he lacked company because he was rejected by people. Another option is to take the genitive as indicating genus or larger class (i.e., &quot;one lacking among men&quot;). In this case one could translate, &quot;he was a transient&quot; (cf. the use of חָדֵל [khadel] in Ps 39:5 HT [39:4 ET]). 11 tn Heb &quot;like a hiding of the face from him,&quot; i.e., &quot;like one before whom the face is hidden&quot; (see BDB 712 s.v. מַסְתֵּר). 12 sn The servant is likened to a seriously ill person who is shunned by others because of his horrible disease.

1 tn The Hebrew term הוֹי (hoy, &quot;woe, ah&quot;) was used in funeral laments and is often prefixed to judgment oracles for rhetorical effect. But here it appears to be a simple interjection, designed to grab the audience&apos;s attention. Perhaps there is a note of sorrow or pity. See BDB 223 s.v. 2 sn The statement is an oxymoron. Its ironic quality adds to its rhetorical impact. The statement reminds one of the norm (one must normally buy commodities) as it expresses the astounding offer. One might paraphrase the statement: &quot;Come and take freely what you normally have to pay for.&quot;

3 tn Heb &quot;for what is not food.&quot; 4 tn The interrogative particle and the verb &quot;spend&quot; are understood here by ellipsis (note the preceding line). 5 tn Heb &quot;your labor,&quot; which stands by metonymy for that which one earns. 6 tn The infinitive absolute follows the imperative and lends emphasis to the exhortation. 7 tn Heb &quot;good&quot; (so NASB, NIV, NRSV). 8 tn Heb &quot;Let your appetite delight in fine food.&quot; sn Nourishing, fine food here represents the blessings God freely offers. These include forgiveness, a new covenantal relationship with God, and national prominence (see vv. 3-6).

9 tn The jussive with vav (ו) conjunctive following the imperative indicates purpose/result. sn To live here refers to covenantal blessing, primarily material prosperity and national security (see vv. 4-5, 13, and Deut 30:6, 15, 19-20). 10 tn Or &quot;an eternal covenant with.&quot; 11 tn Heb &quot;the reliable expressions of loyalty of David.&quot; The syntactical relationship of חַסְדֵי (khasde, &quot;expressions of loyalty&quot;) to the preceding line is unclear. If the term is appositional to בְּרִית (bÿrit, &quot;covenant&quot;), then the Lord here transfers the promises of the Davidic covenant to the entire nation. Another option is to take חַסְדֵי (khasde) as an adverbial accusative and to translate &quot;according to the reliable covenantal promises.&quot; In this case the new covenantal arrangement proposed here is viewed as an extension or perhaps fulfillment of the Davidic promises. A third option, the one reflected in the above translation, is to take the last line as comparative. In this case the new covenant being proposed is analogous to the Davidic covenant. Verses 4-5, which compare David&apos;s international prominence to what Israel will experience, favors this view. In all three of these interpretations, &quot;David&quot; is an objective genitive; he is the recipient of covenantal promises. A fourth option would be to take David as a subjective genitive and understand the line as giving the basis for the preceding promise: &quot;Then I will make an unconditional covenantal promise to you, because of David&apos;s faithful acts of covenantal loyalty.&quot;
